title: Mohini pours the nectar
hook: the nectar's out, the asuras grab, and Mohini pours it as a gift
carry: amrita is poured as grace, not grabbed
tomorrow: the earth itself sinks into the sea. who goes down for it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the treasures from the sea: one story, read as holy event and inner path, with both readings agreeing on the order. The nectar's finally out, and everyone grabs. Who gets a taste?

The first spoonful of something sweet after a long, hard day: people slow down for it. The pot of amrita is out of the sea, carried by Dhanvantari, and the moment it appears, the asuras grab it. They pulled half the rope; they want it all. The gods can't win it back by force. Then a woman walks into the middle of the quarrel, so lovely that everyone stops arguing.
screen: `THE FIRST SWEET SPOONFUL.` → `THE ASURAS GRAB THE POT.` → `A WOMAN WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: She's Mohini, Vishnu in a new form. In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, the asuras hand her the pot themselves and ask her to share it out. She seats the two sides in rows and pours for the gods. One asura, Rahu, slips into the gods' row in disguise and gets a sip. The Sun and the Moon call him out, and Vishnu's discus takes his head. But the nectar has already touched his mouth, so the head lives on; some tellings say that's why, now and then, Rahu swallows the Sun or the Moon: an eclipse. Now the line the Bhagavata doesn't hide. Gods and asuras did the same work, in the same place, on the same rope, and the results weren't the same. The text puts the difference down to one thing: the gods took refuge in Vishnu. The nectar wasn't a wage. It was poured. That's the heart of bhakti, devotion: what matters most comes as grace, received, not grabbed. And you can taste it at the end of a puja, when someone pours a spoonful of panchamrit, the five nectars of milk, curd, ghee, honey and sugar, into your cupped right palm. You don't reach for it. You hold out your hand, and you sip.
screen: `MOHINI POURS THE NECTAR.` · `RAHU SLIPS INTO THE ROW.` · `SAME WORK, DIFFERENT FRUIT.` · `PANCHAMRIT IN YOUR PALM.` · then, large: `POURED, NOT GRABBED.`

segments.voice: If you have water or anything small to eat, first set it in front of you for a moment, the way Hindus offer food to God before eating so it comes back as prasad. Then take one sip or one bite and don't swallow right away. Let it sit on your tongue: the temperature, the taste, what changes as you wait. Then swallow, and notice what stays. If you don't pray, let it simply be a gift you didn't make.
Kurma: the tortoise who held the mountain so the nectar could come up at last.
Hold onto this one: amrita is poured as grace, not grabbed. Hold out your hand. Rest well.

howItsDone: At the end of many pujas, panchamrit is poured into the cupped right palm and sipped as prasad; the story of Mohini and the amrita is retold from the Bhagavata Purana, and in some places Rahu is named in traditional explanations of eclipses.

fork.setup: after puja, your aunt is pouring panchamrit into everyone's palm. your little cousin grabs the spoon to serve himself. by the churning, what's off?
options: it's given, not taken: you hold out your hand and receive it.
nothing; it's the same panchamrit either way.
he should wait until the adults have eaten first.
fork.reveal: the asuras grabbed the pot; Mohini poured. in bhakti what matters most comes as grace, so prasad is received in an open palm.

original.note: Sanskrit amrita: the nectar the whole churning was for.

trapdoor: what you thought: the gods simply win the nectar by being stronger.
what it means: the work was equal; the nectar was poured for those who took refuge in Vishnu, as grace.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata 8.8–8.9, Mohini and Rahu; the text says the effort was equal and puts the difference down to refuge in Vishnu.
recall: rises from the sea and chooses Vishnu

chat.says: nani offered her kheer to krishna before anyone ate, then served it & called it 'amrita.' dad laughed for the first time since the fight. why offer it first?
options: offered food comes back as prasad: a gift poured out, like the amrita.
so the kheer has time to cool before people eat it.
it's just a rule; you get in trouble if you eat first.
chat.meaning: In the churning the amrita was poured by Vishnu, not won. Food offered to God comes back as prasad, a gift, which is why Nani calls her kheer amrita.

tie.story: When the asuras grabbed the amrita, Vishnu as Mohini took the pot and poured it for the gods who had taken refuge in him.
tie.friend: Priya can see Nani's kheer, offered first, comes back as prasad: grace poured out for a family the day after a fight.
tie.you: what did you receive this week that you didn't earn?

Mohini.meaning: Vishnu's lovely form who shares out the nectar

Rahu.meaning: the asura who sneaks a sip of nectar

Dhanvantari.meaning: physician of the gods, who carries the amrita

asuras.meaning: the gods' rivals, who grab the pot

panchamrit.meaning: the five nectars, given as prasad after puja

prasad.meaning: food offered to God and given back as a blessing

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.8–8.9 (the asuras seize the amrita; Mohini; Rahu in the gods' row; the Sun and Moon; the discus; equal effort, different results)
